newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS- Outlook murky,but US still top choice.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS- Outlook murky,but US still top choice.

text.p: An unwelcome jump in U.S. data last week has clipped the wings of bond markets across the board, but U.S. will still fare better than Europe longer term, analysts said on Monday.
"Over both markets there is a shadow overhanging this week," said Adrian Owens, European economist at Bank Julius Baer in London, pointing to possible rate hikes in Germany and the UK.
"I feel that any upside for bond markets in both Europe and U.S. is fairly limited... yields will probably drift higher," he added.
But analysts said the 10-year T-note/Bund spread could still shrink to 50 basis points by the end of the year after swelling to about 75 near term from 66 now.

Spooked by a raft of strong U.S. data on Friday, bonds plunged almost everywhere as investors, clawing new highs in an inflation-free bubble, woke up to the prospect of a rumbling third quarter in the U.S. economy.
The first warning came from the July non-farm payrolls which jumped to 316,000 against a consensus forecast of 193,000, and the unemployment rate, which eased further to 4.8 percent.

The last straw, and the most significant, was the NAPM monthly business survey that showed a steep rise in its headline index to 58.6 percent in July from 55.7 in June. Price indices also ticked higher.
"I think the Treasury market probably peaked at three p.m. (British summer time) last Friday," said Ian Morris, international economist at HSBC James Capel in London.

"We don't expect it to break out of the six to seven pct range, but (30-year) yields will be heading up probably towards 6.75 percent or a bit higher in the next two months." The U.S. long bond currently yields 6.45 percent.
A flood of Treasury issues this week will also be a dampener, but demand outweighs supply by far and the offer should be well-absorbed, analysts said.

Analysts now reckon the much-feared third quarter bounce back in the U.S. economy after a second quarter lull is coming through strongly, with both consumer and industrial sectors showing robust growth.
But it could still take a year before these translate to inflation.
Moreover, prospects in Europe are no better, they say, especially with possible rate hikes this week clouding the near term horizon even for star performers like Italy.
The Bundesbank may use its first opportunity on Tuesday to set variable-rate repo tenders, allowing rates to push up a touch and underpin the soggy mark from near-eight-year lows against the dollar.
German industrial production rose by 1.4 percent in June from May, in line with expectations, and analysts said industrial strength would unlikely to feed into consumer demand just yet.
"In Europe it's more stock building than anything else, so European bonds could outperform the U.S. in the short term," said HSBC's Morris.
But Treasuries, once over the rate hike hump, would resume their rally in the fourth quarter, narrowing the gap to Bunds.
Owens meanwhile favoured the short end of the European peripheral bonds, such as the two-five year sector in Italy, for medium term value. But the timing was crucial.
German rate fears were having a disproportionate impact on the Italian market, and peripherals could initially do worse than core Europe.
"I'd sit for a few days and then I'd see value and I would buy that market," said Owens.

Adam Chester, international bond stategist at Yamaichi International Europe in London, saw long-term Treasury yields back up at 6.50 percent in the near term, but this should tempt long term investors, he said.
"As long as inflation numbers continue to be subdued, people will be able to shake off any stronger data," he said, adding that yields would slide again to 6.25 percent.
